Your synagogue community isn't just a group of people—it's a *shared ethical framework*. When you consistently turn to trusted mentors, rabbis, or peers who share your values, you're internalizing a *lattice of wisdom*. Over time, their voices become part of your own moral compass. - *Example*: When you prayerfully recite the Shema daily, you're not just reciting words—you're reinforcing a core identity. Similarly, when you discuss decisions with community members who embody *chesed* ( kindness) or *tzedek* ( justice), those principles become ingrained in *your* decision-making process. - **Result**: You *do* trust yourself more because you've built a "inner rabbi" who speaks with the wisdom of your community. 2. **"Two are better than one... for if they fall, one will lift up his companion"** ( Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). A tight-knit community provides emotional safety. When you know others have your back, you feel braver to *try* things. This builds confidence *because* you're not alone in the risk. - *Example*: If you're considering a career change, having community members who've navigated similar transitions can give you courage to take the leap. Their support isn't * replacing* your trust in yourself—it's * fueling* it. --- ### **The Risk (When Over-Reliance *Erodes* Self-Trusting)** 1. **"External locus of control" syndrome** (psychological term).
